claims.text: The initial material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloy.
The as-deposited material has a coarse-grained or bulk-like microstructure.
The as-deposited material has pronounced domain-wall pinning.
The baseline alloy exhibits a sharp, hysteretic, first-order magnetostructural transition.
Thin-film sputtering followed by rapid thermal annealing will produce a nanostructured state with reduced grain size.
Reduced grain size will increase the density of interfaces and nanograin boundaries.
The increased interface density will lower the effective density of domain-wall pinning sites.
Interfaces and smaller grains reduce magnetocrystalline defects that trap or impede domain walls.
Microstructural sites can serve as barriers to domain-wall motion and contribute to irreversible magnetic behavior.
Reducing domain-wall pinning will make domain reorientation smoother and more reversible during field cycling.
More reversible domain reorientation will broaden and smooth the magnetocaloric transition.
More reversible domain reorientation will reduce magnetic hysteresis during low-field cooling cycles.
The nano-engineered film will have a less abrupt magnetocaloric response, a broader transition, and a smaller hysteresis loop than the as-deposited baseline.
The thin-film geometry will enable more rapid and efficient heat exchange because of its higher surface-to-volume ratio.
The predicted effects apply under sub-Tesla fields and near the magnetostructural transition temperature.
The predicted effects may fail when film thickness or annealing time and temperature lie far outside the range that produces the desired nanostructure.
Magnetization-versus-temperature and magnetization-versus-field measurements can be used to characterize magnetic transitions and field response.
Failure of enhanced nanostructuring to reproducibly decrease hysteresis, broaden the transition, or correlate with reduced pinning would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as coarse-grained, bulk-like, and explicitly as an as-deposited bulk alloy, while the experimental design refers to a non-treated as-deposited baseline within a sputtered thin-film series. It is therefore unclear whether the control is a bulk specimen or an as-deposited sputtered film; a bulk-to-annealed-film comparison would change both geometry and annealing rather than isolate one intervention.
